title: Diffusion learning reveals viable parameter manifolds and compensation geometry in biological dynamical systems

paper.title: Diffusion learning reveals viable parameter manifolds and compensation geometry in biological dynamical systems
paper.abstract:
Abstract Models of complex systems often have many parameters, yet are constrained by far fewer experimentally accessible observables: similar activity can emerge from coordinated parameter changes. We formalize these compatible parameter sets as viable parameter manifolds : the inverse images of a system’s target dynamical behaviors under a parameter-to-feature map. The relevant codimension is not the number of reported features, but the effective rank of that map at the target scale. Co-varying features lower the codimension, while poor conditioning, high curvature, or regime mixing degrade learnability. We train conditional score-based diffusion models on simulated parameter–feature pairs and use them as amortized samplers of prior-weighted viable sets. In the Lorenz system, scalar trajectory statistics generate thin viable sheets, and two-feature conditioning localizes a transition-adjacent corridor. In the Izhikevich neuron model, four firing descriptors lie close to a nearly two-dimensional family of features, and the learned inverse images reveal distinct regular and irregular compensation geometries. In a recent ODE reduction of finite spiking networks, the same framework reveals excitatory–inhibitory compensation, timescale–coupling tradeoffs, and input-dependent viable manifolds across 4–12 parameter dimensions. In this view, robustness, compensation, and hidden parameter dependencies are
organized as inverse geometry, with diffusion models providing practical tools
for sampling, visualizing, and interrogating that geometry.

sections.heading: Significance Statement
sections.text: Biological dynamical systems often admit many parameter combinations that produce the same function. We show that these non-unique inverse solutions form structured viable parameter manifolds whose dimension, tangent directions, curvature, and multimodality quantify how observables constrain the underlying dynamics. Conditional diffusion models learn these manifolds directly from simulation data in Lorenz, Izhikevich, and neuronal network models. The learned geometry reveals compensation laws, hidden parameter couplings, and the number of effective degrees of freedom that remain after the function is fixed. By turning robustness from a qualitative observation into a measurable geometric object, this framework provides a practical route to analyzing degeneracy and mechanism in complex biological models. Keywords: diffusion models; viable parameter manifold; robustness; compensation geometry; computational neuroscience; dynamical systems

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A central lesson from biological dynamics is that function can be reproducible even when the parameters that generate it are not. Neurons with different conductance combinations can fire in similar ways, networks with different synaptic couplings can produce comparable population activity, and systems biology models often preserve output while many microscopic parameters vary over wide ranges [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Across fields, this phenomenon appears as sloppiness, model-manifold compression, structural non-identifiability, dynamical compensation, and biological degeneracy [ 7 , 6 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 1 ] . This degeneracy is not merely a nuisance for parameter estimation. It is one mechanism by which biological systems remain robust, adaptable, and evolvable [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 2 , 5 ] . Yet most inverse analyses still report isolated parameter fits, local sensitivities, or low-dimensional sweeps, leaving the full shape of the compatible parameter set largely unseen. We propose that the natural object of study is the viable parameter manifold : the set of parameters that realizes a specified dynamical behavior. If 𝜽 ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ k \bm{\theta}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} denotes model parameters and ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) \mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta}) denotes a low-dimensional vector of statistics extracted from simulated dynamics, then a target behavior y y defines ℳ y = { 𝜽 ∈ Θ : ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) = y } . \mathcal{M}_{y}=\{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta:\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})=y\}. (1) Within a fixed dynamical regime, the statistics ℐ \mathcal{I} often vary smoothly with the parameters, so ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} is locally a level set. This simple observation changes the inverse problem. Instead of asking which parameter configuration is best, we study the viable parameter manifold as the inverse image of the parameter-to-feature map, ℳ y = ℐ − 1 ​ ( y ) \mathcal{M}_{y}=\mathcal{I}^{-1}(y) . Then we inquire the geometrical features of ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} , namely the number of (local) dimensions, how it bends, and whether it splits into multiple mechanistic branches. This geometric viewpoint gives direct scientific meaning to quantities that are otherwise treated as technical details. Intrinsic dimension estimates the number of effective degrees of freedom that remain after fixing a target behavior. Tangent spaces encode compensation laws, i.e., infinitesimal parameter co-variations that preserve the same output. Curvature measures how these laws change across the viable set. Nearby level sets show how changes in the desired behavior moves through parameter space. Disconnected components or irregular folds suggest that the chosen observables may be mixing distinct dynamical regimes, often near bifurcations or attractor transitions. Thus, the viable-manifold language used here gives an inverse-geometric way to connect parameter nonuniqueness to prior work on robustness, adaptability, and evolvability [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . The computational challenge is that these manifolds are embedded in parameter spaces that are too large for exhaustive sweeps and too structured for pointwise optimization because of the curse of dimensionality. Conditional score-based diffusion models offer a practical way to uncover and to represent them. We train a diffusion model on simulated parameter–feature pairs and then condition the sampler on a target feature vector to generate parameters compatible with that target [ 16 , 17 ] . Recent theory helps explain why this is plausible: under suitable regularity assumptions, score-based diffusion can adapt to smooth low-dimensional manifold structure without explicitly estimating the manifold [ 18 ] . In our setting, diffusion is therefore used as an amortized sampler of inverse geometry rather than a black-box optimizer. We develop this view across three dynamical systems of increasing complexity and biological relevance. In the Lorenz system [ 19 ] , scalar trajectory statistics generate thin viable sheets and provide a controlled calibration of the geometry. In the Izhikevich neuron model [ 20 , 21 ] , target firing statistics reveal parameter manifolds whose tangent directions express compensatory changes among excitability, reset, and adaptation parameters. In dsODE reductions of finite spiking networks [ 22 ] , viable manifolds expose how excitatory–inhibitory balance extends beyond two-dimensional sweeps to hidden dependencies among synaptic strengths, timescales, connection probabilities, and external drives. Across these systems, the central message is the same: compatible parameters are not a cloud of arbitrary alternatives. They are organized geometric objects, and learning their geometry turns robustness from a qualitative observation into a measurable structure.

sections.heading: 2.1 A regular inverse-geometry framework for viable parameter manifolds
sections.text: The object we seek to learn is not a single fitted parameter vector but the inverse geometry of a dynamical model. Consider a dynamical system with k k parameters 𝒙 ˙ = f ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝜽 ) , 𝜽 ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ k , \dot{\bm{x}}=f(\bm{x},\bm{\theta}),\qquad\bm{\theta}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{k}, (2) and let ℐ : Θ → ℝ m \mathcal{I}:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a vector of dynamical statistics computed from simulated trajectories. For a target feature value y y , the compatible parameters form the viable set ℳ y = { 𝜽 ∈ Θ : ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) = y } , and ℳ y , ε = { 𝜽 ∈ Θ : ‖ ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) − y ‖ ≤ ε } \mathcal{M}_{y}=\{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta:\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})=y\},\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{M}_{y,\varepsilon}=\{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta:\left\lVert\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})-y\right\rVert\leq\varepsilon\} (3) for exact and tolerance-thickened conditioning, respectively. Fig. 1 A illustrates this inverse view: a low-dimensional feature landscape is cut by target values, and each cut can select one or several viable components in parameter space. Throughout the main analysis, we make one explicit local regularity approximation. For a chosen target and sampling neighborhood, we treat the generated parameters as lying within a single dynamical regime. Under this approximation, the long-time statistics used as target features depend smoothly on 𝜽 \bm{\theta} , and a diffusion model conditioned on y y should return samples close to a smooth level-set manifold. This assumption is deliberately local rather than global. When it fails, the failure is itself informative: split clouds, strong folding, abrupt changes in intrinsic dimension, or unstable local tangent spaces suggest that the target neighborhood crosses a bifurcation, mixes multiple attractor branches, or uses summaries that do not fully separate dynamical regimes. The number of independent constraints imposed by the target is the effective rank of the parameter-to-feature map, not the nominal number of reported features. Let σ 1 ​ ( 𝜽 ) ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ q ​ ( 𝜽 ) \sigma_{1}(\bm{\theta})\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{q}(\bm{\theta}) , with q = min ⁡ { k , m } q=\min\{k,m\} , denote the singular values of D ​ ℐ ​ ( 𝜽 ) D\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta}) . At the numerical tolerance of an experiment, we define r y r_{y} as the number of singular directions resolved above feature noise, simulation error, and target tolerance. If r y r_{y} is locally constant on a viable component and the active singular values are bounded away from zero at that scale, the constant-rank theorem gives a local inverse image of dimension k − r y k-r_{y} . Thus, a four-dimensional feature vector may impose only two active constraints if two features co-vary, whereas a scalar feature typically produces a codimension-1 sheet when it is regular. This statement about rank is the entry point to the geometry used throughout this paper. Neighboring level sets ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} show how changes in target behavior move through parameter space. Intrinsic dimension estimates how many parameter degrees of freedom remain after imposing the target. At a regular point, the tangent space T 𝜽 ​ ℳ y = ker ⁡ D ​ ℐ ​ ( 𝜽 ) T_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{M}_{y}=\ker D\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta}) (4) contains the infinitesimal compensation directions: first-order parameter co-variations that preserve the requested behavior. The normal directions, spanned by the active rows of D ​ ℐ ​ ( 𝜽 ) D\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta}) , point toward changes in the target statistics. Curvature measures how these compensation laws change along the viable set; a nearly flat sheet corresponds to an approximately linear tradeoff, whereas a curved manifold indicates that parameter compensation differs across regions. Fig. 1 D serves as a visual glossary for these readouts: neighboring level sets, a local tangent approximation with an across-target direction, and an intrinsic-dimension estimate from a generated cloud. Operational regularity checks. We interpret a target-conditioned cloud as a regular viable manifold when, at the sampling scale, (i) the feature map is smooth within the regime being analyzed; (ii) the active rank of D ​ ℐ D\mathcal{I} is locally stable, even if the nominal features are redundant; (iii) curvature and target-thickening are small enough that local tangent estimates are meaningful; and (iv) connected components can be analyzed directly or chart-wise. When these checks fail, the generated cloud is not discarded. Its irregularity becomes evidence for regime mixing, bifurcation proximity, insufficient observables, or the need for a component-wise atlas. The practical workflow follows this geometry. We fisrt construct a library by randomly sampling parameters, simulating the system, and summarizing the dynamics. then we train a conditional score-based diffusion model on pairs ( 𝜽 , ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) ) (\bm{\theta},\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})) . The score network receives the current noisy parameter state, the target feature vector, and a diffusion-time embedding, and returns a parameter update used in an annealed Langevin sampler (Fig. 1 B). Reverse diffusion then transforms an initially random parameter cloud into a target-conditioned cloud concentrated near the viable set (Fig. 1 C). Unlike local optimization, which returns one or a few solutions, the diffusion sampler approximates an entire conditional family of viable parameters. This conditional family is not automatically a uniform distribution on ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} . Generated samples usually represent a prior-weighted, tolerance-thickened empirical atlas of the viable set (more in SI). Accordingly, the learned parameter set and all its geometric features should be validated by direct re-simulation rather than by raw sample density alone, with diffusion-validation iterations repeated until the learned parameter set converges. Here, we focus on a first-round demonstration rather than on exhaustive iterative refinement of each target-conditioned set. Our goal is not to recover a fully converged viable set for every single target, but to introduce a generative approach to viable-manifolds learning and demonstrate how it facilitates mechanistic analysis for modelers. sections.heading: 2.3 Izhikevich neurons: viable manifolds organize firing statistics beyond categorical classes
sections.text: We next turn to the Izhikevich model. It is a canonical reduced, two-dimensional neuron model of the neuronal membrane potential v v and a recovery variable u u . Using only four dynamical parameters and a reset rule, the Izhikevich model reproduces diverse firing patterns, including tonic spiking, adaptation, bursting, and irregular responses [ 20 , 21 ] : v ˙ = 0.04 ​ v 2 + 5 ​ v + 140 − u + I , u ˙ = a ⁡ ( b ​ v − u ) , \dot{v}=0.04v^{2}+5v+140-u+I,\qquad\dot{u}=a(bv-u), (6) and a reset rule v ↦ c v\mapsto c , u ↦ u + d u\mapsto u+d whenever v ≥ 30 v\geq 30 mV [ 21 ] . The parameters a , b , c , d a,b,c,d model respectively the recovery time constant, sensitivity to subthreshold fluctuations, the nominal voltage reset value, and the post-spike reset of the recovery variable. We fixed the input step current at I = 20 I=20 to examine the diverse spiking patterns accessible within a simple stimulation protocol. We start by conditioning on a four-component target. After discarding the first 50 ms of initial transients, we summarized spikes in the 50–200 ms applied current window by firing rate, mean inter-spike interval (ISI), coefficient of variation (CV) of the ISI, and Fano factor (Fig. 3 A). Firing rate is spike count divided by window duration; mean ISI and CV(ISI) summarize spike-to-spike timing; and Fano factor summarizes count variability across 10-ms bins. We chose these standard descriptors because they are both widely used observables in analyses of cortical and single-neuron spiking [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] . Were these four targets to act as independent, locally transverse constraints, one might expect the inverse images in ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) to shrink to isolated points, or to small tolerance-broadened clouds. Instead, the relevant quantity proves to be the effective rank of the target family. This is because firing rate and mean ISI encode the timescale of the output. In contrast, CV(ISI) and Fano factor measure temporal irregularity and count variability. Across randomly sampled responses filtered to 20–200 Hz, the four reported statistics lie close to a nearly two-dimensional surface: the first two principal components explain 52.2 % 52.2\% and 37.9 % 37.9\% of the variance, respectively (Fig. 3 B). The nominally four-dimensional feature target is therefore closer to a two-constraint object in the sampled regimes, so codimension-two viable sets are the generic inverse geometry. That lower effective dimension appears directly in parameter space. Target-conditioned diffusion generates thin, structured subsets of ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) that pass through held-out original parameters and reproduce their target feature vectors under direct simulation (Fig. 3 C,D). The irregular medium-rate target in Fig. 3 C ( 107 107 Hz, 9.7 9.7 ms, CV 0.80 0.80 , Fano 0.93 0.93 ) occupies a visibly curved sheet, whereas the more regular target ( 193 193 Hz, 5.3 5.3 ms, CV 0.31 0.31 , Fano 0.31 0.31 ) is narrower and closer to an affine strip. Their participation-ratio dimensions, 2.08 2.08 and 1.74 1.74 , are consistent with a four-parameter model constrained by a feature family with effective dimension near two. They are viable manifolds with clear geometrical features, not merely noisy balls around a reference point. Two observations are especially relevant for neuroscience. First, tangent spaces at points on the manifolds reveal the first-order compensation geometry : local co-variation of ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) that preserves firing statistics. Second, nearby feature targets produce nearby manifolds, indicating that the model learned a smoothly varying family of viable sets rather than memorizing discrete templates. Thus, the learned manifolds can be viewed as population-of-models descriptions of neuronal degeneracy and homeostatic compensation, revealing dependencies among excitability, recovery, reset, and adaptation parameters [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 29 ] . As a second-order geometric descriptor, curvature measures how a local compensation law changes along the manifold. In our generated irregular-firing manifolds, several projections have negative curvature, which we interpret as an antagonistic compensation pattern in those coordinates: larger movement in one parameter direction requires an increasingly strong offset in another to preserve the target features. The reset/adaptation interpretation below is derived from the local spike-to-spike map analysis in the SI Appendix. Biologically, this suggests that irregular firing is maintained by balancing reset-driven excitability against adaptation-driven memory or stability. These competing influences pull the manifold in different directions and allow the Izhikevich model to produce diverse spiking patterns. As a validation, parameter configurations generated from these manifolds reproduce irregular firing patterns and statistics similar to the target dynamics (Fig. 3 D). The seemingly linear parameter manifolds for regular spiking admit a sharper dynamical interpretation (Fig. 3 E). Under constant input within the stimulation window, the hybrid flow reduces spike-to-spike dynamics to a one-dimensional return map for the post-spike recovery value. Regular spiking corresponds to a stable fixed point of this adaptation map, so fixing the target firing rate or mean ISI and low irregularity imposes approximately two independent smooth constraints on ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) : one on the inter-spike time interval from the reset c c to the threshold, and another on the balance amongst the spike-triggered recovery increment d d , the recovery timescale a a , and the subthreshold coupling b b . Linearizing these constraints around a stable periodic orbit yields local compensation laws of the form A a ​ δ ​ a + A b ​ δ ​ b + A c ​ δ ​ c + A d ​ δ ​ d ≈ 0 A_{a}\delta a+A_{b}\delta b+A_{c}\delta c+A_{d}\delta d\approx 0 , so the viable set is well approximated by a small affine chart. Consistent with this picture, the regular-firing family remains two-dimensional and becomes increasingly ribbon-like as the rate increases. sections.heading: 2.4 dsODE synaptic manifolds extend E–I landscape geometry into network inverse problems
sections.text: We next moved to dsODE, a deterministic reduction of finite-sized spiking neuronal networks (SNN). dsODE uses a discretized voltage-bin structure to represent the population voltage configuration of the SNN, and uses pending synaptic variables to describe the recurrent drives to neuron populations. In different sweeps of the parameter space, dsODE reveals and faithfully reproduces fixed points, one-beat and multi-beat oscillations, coexistence of multiple attractors, and the bifurcation organization of the underlying spiking network model [ 22 ] . These properties make dsODE an especially useful testbed for inverse problems: it remains mechanistically tied to SNN dynamics, yet is light enough to support the large simulation libraries needed for conditional generation. Without a reduction of this kind, broad parameter evaluations at the level of the full SNN would be computationally prohibitive, especially if one wishes to preserve the attractor and bifurcation structure that organizes viable solutions [ 30 , 22 ] . The basic construction of dsODE and a few of the representative activities (the “one-beat” and “two-beat” oscillations) are summarized in Fig. 4 . Fig. 4: dsODE schematic and representative population activity. (A) Excitatory and inhibitory populations with recurrent coupling ranges. (B-D) Representative E/I rate traces (upper) and voltage-bin view of population activity at the time section indicated by black vertical lines (lower). We begin with the four recurrent synaptic coupling strengths ( S E ​ E , S I ​ E , S E ​ I , S I ​ I ) (S_{EE},S_{IE},S_{EI},S_{II}) because these are precisely the parameters to which the overall network dynamics is most sensitive. Xiao et al. showed that the viable firing-rate region is thin in this synaptic-strength landscape, so single-parameter perturbations of order 1 % 1\% can already leave the viable set [ 30 ] , while dsODE showed that varying these same couplings organizes a much richer set of dynamical regimes [ 22 ] . Following Xiao et al., we analyzed the four-dimensional synaptic box in the inhibition-plane coordinates ( S I ​ E / S I ​ I , S E ​ I / S E ​ E ) (S_{IE}/S_{II},S_{EI}/S_{EE}) , whose product acts as a suppression index for E-cells. In the background-regime analysis, excitatory and inhibitory mean rates remain tightly linked near the mean-field relation, so the nominal two-rate target behaves effectively as a single active constraint. The corresponding viable set is therefore close to codimension-1 in the four-dimensional synaptic space and appears as hyperbolic viable strips in the inhibition plane, consistent with Fig. 1A of Xiao et al. [30] ; the left panel of Fig. 5 B reproduces that landscape. We recovered this result with dsODE in the same regime (SI Appendix), where participation-ratio dimensions are 2.5–2.9, close to the three-dimensional expectation. We then moved to a more driven regime, where E and I mean rates are less tightly coupled and therefore provide two less dependent constraints (Fig. 5 A middle). The learned mean-conditioned families become intrinsically thinner, with participation-ratio dimensions between about 1 and 2.2, even though their projection onto the inhibition plane remains strip-like. Direct re-simulation confirms recovery of the target mean rates (Fig. 5 A right). In this sense, the same inhibitory-balance mechanism still organizes the projection, but the intrinsic dimension now reflects the number of firing rate directions that are genuinely independent. This already suggests that once temporal heterogeneity (e.g., oscillations or bursting behavior) becomes appreciable, mean rates alone may not fully resolve the viable structure in this synaptic box. As in the one-beat and two-beat dynamics reported previously [ 22 , 31 ] , our simulations show that distinct oscillatory families can have similar long-time average E/I rates while differing strongly in temporal modulation amplitude. We therefore next conditioned on the standard deviations (std) of the excitatory and inhibitory rates. The resulting families in Fig. 5 B differ qualitatively from the mean-conditioned ones: they can split, becoming visibly multimodal in the same inhibition plane, even though direct re-simulation still validates the requested std targets. Parameter configurations located in different clusters correspond to 1-beat and 2-beat oscillatory dynamics, respectively (Fig. 5 B right). We regard that irregularity as informative rather than as a failure of the generator. Conditional manifold learning is easiest when the inverse support varies smoothly with the target locally, but near bifurcations that support can fold or split because nearby parameters lie on different dynamical branches while possibly maintaining similar low-order summaries. Mean-conditioned sets therefore tend to remain close to the single compensation strip imposed by E–I balance, whereas std-conditioned sets are more branch-sensitive and can separate distinct dynamical regimes, e.g., one-beat from two-beat responses. Finally, we find that overlapping mean- and std-conditioned manifolds collapse to compact local neighborhoods around held-out original parameters on the inhibition plane and generate temporally similar trajectories within each branch (Fig. 5 C). Consistent with this view, these neighborhoods are approximately ellipsoidal in projection, closer to Gaussian-like clusters than to long compensation strips. Thus, low-order moments do not merely tighten a point estimate; taken together, they localize branch-specific viable parameter sets while revealing the nearby regime structure that perturbs an otherwise smooth manifold geometry. sections.heading: 2.5 Higher-dimensional dsODE manifolds reveal hidden dependencies among coupling, timescale, and drive
sections.text: SNN dynamics depend not only on synaptic coupling weights but also on synaptic timescales, external drive, and other model parameters. We therefore ask how these physiological and anatomical parameters are organized to produce similar dynamics. We imposed the same four observables—the means and standard deviations of the excitatory and inhibitory firing rates—and tracked the resulting viable manifolds as we expanded the dsODE parameter space to 8, 10, and 12 dimensions, to reveal hidden compensation among coupling, timescale, and drive. We first focus on an eight-dimensional parameter space comprising four synaptic strengths ( S Q ​ R S_{QR} ) and four synaptic timescales ( τ Q ​ R \tau_{QR} ). sections.heading: 2.6 Dimensionality and regularity determine both learnability and interpretation
sections.text: Across all three systems, the same principle appears repeatedly: diffusion learns viable sets most effectively when the target-conditioned inverse family is both low-dimensional and regular at the tolerance scale. This is precisely where the method becomes computationally useful. Let ℐ : Θ → ℝ r y \mathcal{I}:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{r_{y}} be the feature map, with Θ ⊂ ℝ k \Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} . Assume the target coordinates are locally rank ​ D ​ ℐ = r y \mathrm{rank}\,D\mathcal{I}=r_{y} at the solution set, and the viable set ℐ − 1 ​ ( y ∗ ) \mathcal{I}^{-1}(y^{\ast}) has intrinsic dimension d = k − r y d=k-r_{y} . In a bounded parameter box, an ε \varepsilon -tube around such a set occupies only an O ⁡ ( ε r y ) O(\varepsilon^{r_{y}}) fraction of the ambient volume. Therefore, unguided rejection or nearest-neighbor search pays a penalty in the normal directions before it ever resolves the tangential geometry. By contrast, conditional diffusion amortizes the need for simulation in parameter space: one simulation library can be reused across many nearby target queries, and inference becomes direct proposal generation followed by re-simulation validation. More importantly, the cost of building the library can itself be reduced by the regularity of the viable set and is therefore not fully described by a naive exponential-in- d d grid law. Recent theory shows that score-based diffusion can adapt to smooth low-dimensional manifold structure without explicitly estimating the manifold. In particular, under suitable regularity assumptions, forward–backward diffusion achieves the minimax-optimal W 1 W_{1} rate, up to logarithmic factors, max ( n − 1 / 2 , n − ( α + 1 ) / ( 2 α + d ) ) , \max\!\left(n^{-1/2},\,n^{-(\alpha+1)/(2\alpha+d)}\right), for distributions with an α \alpha -smooth density supported on a d d -dimensional manifold [ 18 ] . Thus, smoother target distributions yield better rates, and regular single-sheet manifolds generally require less data than folded, kinked, or multimodal inverse sets. In the extreme case of a completely smooth target set ( α \alpha dominating d d ), cost of constructing library does not scale exponentially with dimension. A more thorough comparison between diffusion-based manifold computation and classical alternatives is provided in the SI. Fig. 7 summarizes this contraction effect visually. In dsODE, conditioning successively on E-rate mean alone, on both E/I means, and then on E/I means together with E/I standard deviations contracts and separates the generated four-dimensional synaptic clouds projected onto the inhibition plane (Fig. 7 A). For one target, mean-rate conditioning alone still merges two dynamical families, whereas adding component-specific standard-deviation guidance resolves them into distinct clouds with different beat traces. The same pattern appears in the simpler systems. Recall that in the Lorenz model, scalar features such as x x -std or z z -std leave broader parameter clouds than joint ( x ​ -std , z ​ -std ) (x\text{-std},z\text{-std}) conditioning (Fig. 7 B); in the Izhikevich neuron, rate-only and CV(ISI)-only guidance leave broader clouds than the full four-feature guide (data not shown). The shrinking participation-ratio dimensions directly reflect this compression. Multimodality or disconnected components can flag either genuine regime structure or insufficient observables. The dsODE example in Fig. 7 A makes this concrete: mean-rate guidance alone can merge one-beat and two-beat families, whereas adding standard deviations splits that merged cloud into branch-specific neighborhoods. More generally, richer targets help only when they add independent active information. Adding redundant coordinates to the guide need not lower intrinsic dimension; it may only improve conditioning. By contrast, observables aligned with the active normals of the parameter-to-feature map can contract clouds, separate nearby regimes, and regularize local geometry. This is why target design is itself a scientific issue. The most informative guides are not merely larger feature vectors, but observables that resolve the directions along which biological function actually changes [ 10 , 32 , 11 ] . sections.heading: 3 Discussion
sections.text: This work recasts inverse modeling in dynamical systems as the study of viable parameter manifolds. The typical parameter-fitting task answers one question: can the model reproduce the target? A viable manifold answers a deeper question: In how many mechanistically distinct ways can the model reproduce it and how must parameters co-vary to preserve it? Throughout this study, the compatible parameter sets were not featureless clouds but manifolds with geometry. The geometry matters not only for fitting but also for what a model can generalize, explain, and render interpretable, echoing the sloppy-model view that predictions are controlled by a small number of effective parameter combinations [ 7 , 6 , 33 , 8 , 9 ] . The three case studies play complementary roles. The Lorenz system shows the basic inverse geometry in a classical setting: fixing a scalar trajectory statistic cuts a three-dimensional parameter box into thin 2D sheets. In the Izhikevich model of single-neuron dynamics, four common firing descriptors co-vary strongly rather than acting as four independent constraints, so the inverse images remain extended manifolds in a four-dimensional parameter space. Their tangent directions describe compensatory changes among physiological parameters. The dsODE examples then move from single-neuron compensation to network homeostasis. Mean rates recover excitatory–inhibitory balance-like strips, rate fluctuations split branches that would merge when targeted on mean rates alone. Furthermore, higher-dimensional generations reveal tradeoffs among recurrent strength, filtering timescale, refractory effects, and external drive. In this sense, the learned parameter manifolds provide population-of-models descriptions of neuronal degeneracy and homeostatic compensation rather than opaque families of equally good fits [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 29 ] . A useful way to summarize these results is that degeneracy is not disorder. In biological models, many parameter combinations can produce the same function or behavior, but these combinations are constrained by the key features in the behavior. Intrinsic dimension measures the number of free local parameter directions. Tangent spaces identify the local compensation laws. The relative location of neighboring level sets shows how the function changes as parameters move (local coordinates of tangent spaces and normal directions shown in Fig. 7 C). Curvature tells us when a simple linear compensation rule is only local, and component structure reveals alternative mechanisms or multiple regimes. In this paper these geometric quantities are treated as mechanistic observables extracted from the inverse problem, complementing the forward model-manifold view of sloppy systems [ 33 , 9 , 8 ] . Thus our results also clarify the true goal of target design. Imposing more feature coordinates is useful only when those coordinates add independent active information about the parameter-to-feature map. Conversely, a small number of well-chosen observables resolving the true geometry can sharply contract a viable set or separate dynamical branches if they are well aligned with directions along which the system dynamics actually changes. This regular-manifold viewpoint is deliberately local. Yet parameter spaces of nonlinear systems are not globally smooth in this sense. Bifurcations, coexistence of attractors, transient chaos, and branch switching can match the same low-order statistics with different mechanisms [ 34 , 23 ] . In such cases, irregular diffusion outputs are strong indicators of regime mixing or nearby bifurcation structure, and should trigger targeted simulation, continuation, or component-wise analysis rather than being averaged into a single, smooth manifold. The reader should note that conditional diffusion does not remove the need for simulation nor guarantee uniform sampling on a level set. Therefore our framework should not be treated as a universal solver for high-dimensional bifurcation discovery. It is valuable here because diffusion amortizes inverse queries and returns structured candidate sets that can be validated and analyzed geometrically. This perspective connects several traditions that are often separated. The sloppy/model-manifold literature studies forward images in prediction space, whereas identifiability and dynamical-compensation theory emphasize inverse non-uniqueness; viable manifolds unify these viewpoints as inverse geometric objects [ 33 , 9 , 10 , 32 , 11 ] . From dynamical systems, it inherits the idea that qualitative regimes organize parameter space. From inverse problems, it inherits the importance of pre-images and identifiability. From neuroscience, it inherits the problem of robustness and degeneracy in neurons and circuits. From modern generative modeling, it gains a scalable way to sample complicated embedded sets. This synthesis suggests a broader program: building regime-aware atlases of viable manifolds, using active learning to refine transition-adjacent strata, and combining diffusion samplers with classical continuation methods to trace bifurcation surfaces when the smooth-manifold assumption fails. The natural next step is therefore regime-aware inverse geometry. Promising directions include component-wise manifold learning, active refinement of transition-adjacent strata, and diffusion-assisted continuation along codimension-1 boundaries. The main conceptual conclusion is that robust biological function corresponds to a structured space of possibilities rather than to a privileged parameter configuration. Learning that space makes robustness measurable, compensation visible, and hidden dependencies testable. Viable parameter manifolds therefore turn inverse modeling from the search for one answer into the analysis of the space of answers. By connecting modern generative modeling to classical dynamical-systems ideas, this study establishes a technical language for a core principle: that complex dynamical systems maintain robust function amid parameter variability through structured, low-dimensional mechanisms that we can now extract and analyze.

sections.heading: 4.1 Conditional diffusion model
sections.text: We used conditional score-based diffusion models to learn the distribution of parameters 𝜽 \bm{\theta} given target features y = ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) y=\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta}) [ 35 , 36 , 16 , 17 ] . Training data consisted of simulation-labeled parameter samples ( 𝜽 i , y i ) (\bm{\theta}_{i},y_{i}) . In all case studies, the score network was conditioned on both the target feature vector and the diffusion time or noise level, and generated parameters were always checked by direct re-simulation. Parameters and features were linearly normalized before training. At test time, the model was queried with a desired target feature vector and used to generate candidate parameters. The figures report re-simulated generated samples or direct simulations of representative generated parameters rather than raw network output. For Lorenz validation histograms we used 5000 generated parameters per scalar target. For Izhikevich validation traces and histograms we simulated 300 generated neurons per target. For dsODE validation panels, dots and error bars summarize re-simulations of 200 generated parameters per target.

sections.heading: 4.6 Validation and held-out tests
sections.text: For each target, generated parameters were re-simulated and compared with the requested features. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 arXiv:2607.03671v1 [q-bio.QM] 04 Jul 2026 Diffusion learning reveals viable parameter manifolds and compensation geometry in biological dynamical systems Ruilin Zhang Louis Tao Zhuo-Cheng Xiao Abstract Models of complex systems often have many parameters, yet are constrained by far fewer experimentally accessible observables: similar activity can emerge from coordinated parameter changes. We formalize these compatible parameter sets as viable parameter manifolds : the inverse images of a system’s target dynamical behaviors under a parameter-to-feature map. The relevant codimension is not the number of reported features, but the effective rank of that map at the target scale. Co-varying features lower the codimension, while poor conditioning, high curvature, or regime mixing degrade learnability. We train conditional score-based diffusion models on simulated parameter–feature pairs and use them as amortized samplers of prior-weighted viable sets. In the Lorenz system, scalar trajectory statistics generate thin viable sheets, and two-feature conditioning localizes a transition-adjacent corridor. In the Izhikevich neuron model, four firing descriptors lie close to a nearly two-dimensional family of features, and the learned inverse images reveal distinct regular and irregular compensation geometries. In a recent ODE reduction of finite spiking networks, the same framework reveals excitatory–inhibitory compensation, timescale–coupling tradeoffs, and input-dependent viable manifolds across 4–12 parameter dimensions. In this view, robustness, compensation, and hidden parameter dependencies are organized as inverse geometry, with diffusion models providing practical tools for sampling, visualizing, and interrogating that geometry. 1 Peking University–Tsinghua University–National Institute of Biological Sciences Joint Graduate Program, Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Studies, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China 2 Center for Bioinformatics, School of Life Sciences, National Laboratory of Protein Engineering and Plant Genetic Engineering, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China 3 Center for Quantitative Biology, Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Studies, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China 4 NYU-ECNU Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China 5 NYU-ECNU Institute of Brain and Cognitive Science, New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China Classification: Applied Mathematics; Dynamical Systems; Computational Neuroscience Significance Statement Biological dynamical systems often admit many parameter combinations that produce the same function. We show that these non-unique inverse solutions form structured viable parameter manifolds whose dimension, tangent directions, curvature, and multimodality quantify how observables constrain the underlying dynamics. Conditional diffusion models learn these manifolds directly from simulation data in Lorenz, Izhikevich, and neuronal network models. The learned geometry reveals compensation laws, hidden parameter couplings, and the number of effective degrees of freedom that remain after the function is fixed. By turning robustness from a qualitative observation into a measurable geometric object, this framework provides a practical route to analyzing degeneracy and mechanism in complex biological models. Keywords: diffusion models; viable parameter manifold; robustness; compensation geometry; computational neuroscience; dynamical systems 1 Introduction A central lesson from biological dynamics is that function can be reproducible even when the parameters that generate it are not. Neurons with different conductance combinations can fire in similar ways, networks with different synaptic couplings can produce comparable population activity, and systems biology models often preserve output while many microscopic parameters vary over wide ranges [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Across fields, this phenomenon appears as sloppiness, model-manifold compression, structural non-identifiability, dynamical compensation, and biological degeneracy [ 7 , 6 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 1 ] . This degeneracy is not merely a nuisance for parameter estimation. It is one mechanism by which biological systems remain robust, adaptable, and evolvable [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 2 , 5 ] . Yet most inverse analyses still report isolated parameter fits, local sensitivities, or low-dimensional sweeps, leaving the full shape of the compatible parameter set largely unseen. We propose that the natural object of study is the viable parameter manifold : the set of parameters that realizes a specified dynamical behavior. If 𝜽 ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ k \bm{\theta}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} denotes model parameters and ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) \mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta}) denotes a low-dimensional vector of statistics extracted from simulated dynamics, then a target behavior y y defines ℳ y = { 𝜽 ∈ Θ : ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) = y } . \mathcal{M}_{y}=\{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta:\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})=y\}. (1) Within a fixed dynamical regime, the statistics ℐ \mathcal{I} often vary smoothly with the parameters, so ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} is locally a level set. This simple observation changes the inverse problem. Instead of asking which parameter configuration is best, we study the viable parameter manifold as the inverse image of the parameter-to-feature map, ℳ y = ℐ − 1 ​ ( y ) \mathcal{M}_{y}=\mathcal{I}^{-1}(y) . Then we inquire the geometrical features of ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} , namely the number of (local) dimensions, how it bends, and whether it splits into multiple mechanistic branches. This geometric viewpoint gives direct scientific meaning to quantities that are otherwise treated as technical details. Intrinsic dimension estimates the number of effective degrees of freedom that remain after fixing a target behavior. Tangent spaces encode compensation laws, i.e., infinitesimal parameter co-variations that preserve the same output. Curvature measures how these laws change across the viable set. Nearby level sets show how changes in the desired behavior moves through parameter space. Disconnected components or irregular folds suggest that the chosen observables may be mixing distinct dynamical regimes, often near bifurcations or attractor transitions. Thus, the viable-manifold language used here gives an inverse-geometric way to connect parameter nonuniqueness to prior work on robustness, adaptability, and evolvability [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . The computational challenge is that these manifolds are embedded in parameter spaces that are too large for exhaustive sweeps and too structured for pointwise optimization because of the curse of dimensionality. Conditional score-based diffusion models offer a practical way to uncover and to represent them. We train a diffusion model on simulated parameter–feature pairs and then condition the sampler on a target feature vector to generate parameters compatible with that target [ 16 , 17 ] . Recent theory helps explain why this is plausible: under suitable regularity assumptions, score-based diffusion can adapt to smooth low-dimensional manifold structure without explicitly estimating the manifold [ 18 ] . In our setting, diffusion is therefore used as an amortized sampler of inverse geometry rather than a black-box optimizer. We develop this view across three dynamical systems of increasing complexity and biological relevance. In the Lorenz system [ 19 ] , scalar trajectory statistics generate thin viable sheets and provide a controlled calibration of the geometry. In the Izhikevich neuron model [ 20 , 21 ] , target firing statistics reveal parameter manifolds whose tangent directions express compensatory changes among excitability, reset, and adaptation parameters. In dsODE reductions of finite spiking networks [ 22 ] , viable manifolds expose how excitatory–inhibitory balance extends beyond two-dimensional sweeps to hidden dependencies among synaptic strengths, timescales, connection probabilities, and external drives. Across these systems, the central message is the same: compatible parameters are not a cloud of arbitrary alternatives. They are organized geometric objects, and learning their geometry turns robustness from a qualitative observation into a measurable structure. 2 Results 2.1 A regular inverse-geometry framework for viable parameter manifolds The object we seek to learn is not a single fitted parameter vector but the inverse geometry of a dynamical model. Consider a dynamical system with k k parameters 𝒙 ˙ = f ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝜽 ) , 𝜽 ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ k , \dot{\bm{x}}=f(\bm{x},\bm{\theta}),\qquad\bm{\theta}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{k}, (2) and let ℐ : Θ → ℝ m \mathcal{I}:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a vector of dynamical statistics computed from simulated trajectories. Operational regularity checks. We interpret a target-conditioned cloud as a regular viable manifold when, at the sampling scale, (i) the feature map is smooth within the regime being analyzed; (ii) the active rank of D ​ ℐ D\mathcal{I} is locally stable, even if the nominal features are redundant; (iii) curvature and target-thickening are small enough that local tangent estimates are meaningful; and (iv) connected components can be analyzed directly or chart-wise. When these checks fail, the generated cloud is not discarded. Its irregularity becomes evidence for regime mixing, bifurcation proximity, insufficient observables, or the need for a component-wise atlas. The practical workflow follows this geometry. We fisrt construct a library by randomly sampling parameters, simulating the system, and summarizing the dynamics. then we train a conditional score-based diffusion model on pairs ( 𝜽 , ℐ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) ) (\bm{\theta},\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})) . The score network receives the current noisy parameter state, the target feature vector, and a diffusion-time embedding, and returns a parameter update used in an annealed Langevin sampler (Fig. 1 B). Reverse diffusion then transforms an initially random parameter cloud into a target-conditioned cloud concentrated near the viable set (Fig. 1 C). Unlike local optimization, which returns one or a few solutions, the diffusion sampler approximates an entire conditional family of viable parameters. This conditional family is not automatically a uniform distribution on ℳ y \mathcal{M}_{y} . Generated samples usually represent a prior-weighted, tolerance-thickened empirical atlas of the viable set (more in SI). Accordingly, the learned parameter set and all its geometric features should be validated by direct re-simulation rather than by raw sample density alone, with diffusion-validation iterations repeated until the learned parameter set converges. Here, we focus on a first-round demonstration rather than on exhaustive iterative refinement of each target-conditioned set. Our goal is not to recover a fully converged viable set for every single target, but to introduce a generative approach to viable-manifolds learning and demonstrate how it facilitates mechanistic analysis for modelers. Two red dots on the orange line represent the intersection points. 2.3 Izhikevich neurons: viable manifolds organize firing statistics beyond categorical classes We next turn to the Izhikevich model. It is a canonical reduced, two-dimensional neuron model of the neuronal membrane potential v v and a recovery variable u u . Using only four dynamical parameters and a reset rule, the Izhikevich model reproduces diverse firing patterns, including tonic spiking, adaptation, bursting, and irregular responses [ 20 , 21 ] : v ˙ = 0.04 ​ v 2 + 5 ​ v + 140 − u + I , u ˙ = a ⁡ ( b ​ v − u ) , \dot{v}=0.04v^{2}+5v+140-u+I,\qquad\dot{u}=a(bv-u), (6) and a reset rule v ↦ c v\mapsto c , u ↦ u + d u\mapsto u+d whenever v ≥ 30 v\geq 30 mV [ 21 ] . The parameters a , b , c , d a,b,c,d model respectively the recovery time constant, sensitivity to subthreshold fluctuations, the nominal voltage reset value, and the post-spike reset of the recovery variable. We fixed the input step current at I = 20 I=20 to examine the diverse spiking patterns accessible within a simple stimulation protocol. We start by conditioning on a four-component target. After discarding the first 50 ms of initial transients, we summarized spikes in the 50–200 ms applied current window by firing rate, mean inter-spike interval (ISI), coefficient of variation (CV) of the ISI, and Fano factor (Fig. 3 A). Firing rate is spike count divided by window duration; mean ISI and CV(ISI) summarize spike-to-spike timing; and Fano factor summarizes count variability across 10-ms bins. We chose these standard descriptors because they are both widely used observables in analyses of cortical and single-neuron spiking [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] . Were these four targets to act as independent, locally transverse constraints, one might expect the inverse images in ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) to shrink to isolated points, or to small tolerance-broadened clouds. Instead, the relevant quantity proves to be the effective rank of the target family. This is because firing rate and mean ISI encode the timescale of the output. In contrast, CV(ISI) and Fano factor measure temporal irregularity and count variability. Across randomly sampled responses filtered to 20–200 Hz, the four reported statistics lie close to a nearly two-dimensional surface: the first two principal components explain 52.2 % 52.2\% and 37.9 % 37.9\% of the variance, respectively (Fig. 3 B). The nominally four-dimensional feature target is therefore closer to a two-constraint object in the sampled regimes, so codimension-two viable sets are the generic inverse geometry. That lower effective dimension appears directly in parameter space. Target-conditioned diffusion generates thin, structured subsets of ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) that pass through held-out original parameters and reproduce their target feature vectors under direct simulation (Fig. 3 C,D). The irregular medium-rate target in Fig. 3 C ( 107 107 Hz, 9.7 9.7 ms, CV 0.80 0.80 , Fano 0.93 0.93 ) occupies a visibly curved sheet, whereas the more regular target ( 193 193 Hz, 5.3 5.3 ms, CV 0.31 0.31 , Fano 0.31 0.31 ) is narrower and closer to an affine strip. Their participation-ratio dimensions, 2.08 2.08 and 1.74 1.74 , are consistent with a four-parameter model constrained by a feature family with effective dimension near two. They are viable manifolds with clear geometrical features, not merely noisy balls around a reference point. Two observations are especially relevant for neuroscience. First, tangent spaces at points on the manifolds reveal the first-order compensation geometry : local co-variation of ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) that preserves firing statistics. Second, nearby feature targets produce nearby manifolds, indicating that the model learned a smoothly varying family of viable sets rather than memorizing discrete templates. Thus, the learned manifolds can be viewed as population-of-models descriptions of neuronal degeneracy and homeostatic compensation, revealing dependencies among excitability, recovery, reset, and adaptation parameters [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 29 ] . As a second-order geometric descriptor, curvature measures how a local compensation law changes along the manifold. In our generated irregular-firing manifolds, several projections have negative curvature, which we interpret as an antagonistic compensation pattern in those coordinates: larger movement in one parameter direction requires an increasingly strong offset in another to preserve the target features. The reset/adaptation interpretation below is derived from the local spike-to-spike map analysis in the SI Appendix. Biologically, this suggests that irregular firing is maintained by balancing reset-driven excitability against adaptation-driven memory or stability. These competing influences pull the manifold in different directions and allow the Izhikevich model to produce diverse spiking patterns. As a validation, parameter configurations generated from these manifolds reproduce irregular firing patterns and statistics similar to the target dynamics (Fig. 3 D). The seemingly linear parameter manifolds for regular spiking admit a sharper dynamical interpretation (Fig. 3 E). Under constant input within the stimulation window, the hybrid flow reduces spike-to-spike dynamics to a one-dimensional return map for the post-spike recovery value. Regular spiking corresponds to a stable fixed point of this adaptation map, so fixing the target firing rate or mean ISI and low irregularity imposes approximately two independent smooth constraints on ( a , b , c , d ) (a,b,c,d) : one on the inter-spike time interval from the reset c c to the threshold, and another on the balance amongst the spike-triggered recovery increment d d , the recovery timescale a a , and the subthreshold coupling b b . Linearizing these constraints around a stable periodic orbit yields local compensation laws of the form A a ​ δ ​ a + A b ​ δ ​ b + A c ​ δ ​ c + A d ​ δ ​ d ≈ 0 A_{a}\delta a+A_{b}\delta b+A_{c}\delta c+A_{d}\delta d\approx 0 , so the viable set is well approximated by a small affine chart. Consistent with this picture, the regular-firing family remains two-dimensional and becomes increasingly ribbon-like as the rate increases. In different sweeps of the parameter space, dsODE reveals and faithfully reproduces fixed points, one-beat and multi-beat oscillations, coexistence of multiple attractors, and the bifurcation organization of the underlying spiking network model [ 22 ] . These properties make dsODE an especially useful testbed for inverse problems: it remains mechanistically tied to SNN dynamics, yet is light enough to support the large simulation libraries needed for conditional generation. Without a reduction of this kind, broad parameter evaluations at the level of the full SNN would be computationally prohibitive, especially if one wishes to preserve the attractor and bifurcation structure that organizes viable solutions [ 30 , 22 ] . Xiao et al. showed that the viable firing-rate region is thin in this synaptic-strength landscape, so single-parameter perturbations of order 1 % 1\% can already leave the viable set [ 30 ] , while dsODE showed that varying these same couplings organizes a much richer set of dynamical regimes [ 22 ] . Following Xiao et al., we analyzed the four-dimensional synaptic box in the inhibition-plane coordinates ( S I ​ E / S I ​ I , S E ​ I / S E ​ E ) (S_{IE}/S_{II},S_{EI}/S_{EE}) , whose product acts as a suppression index for E-cells. We therefore next conditioned on the standard deviations (std) of the excitatory and inhibitory rates. The resulting families in Fig. 5 B differ qualitatively from the mean-conditioned ones: they can split, becoming visibly multimodal in the same inhibition plane, even though direct re-simulation still validates the requested std targets. Parameter configurations located in different clusters correspond to 1-beat and 2-beat oscillatory dynamics, respectively (Fig. 5 B right). We regard that irregularity as informative rather than as a failure of the generator. Conditional manifold learning is easiest when the inverse support varies smoothly with the target locally, but near bifurcations that support can fold or split because nearby parameters lie on different dynamical branches while possibly maintaining similar low-order summaries. Mean-conditioned sets therefore tend to remain close to the single compensation strip imposed by E–I balance, whereas std-conditioned sets are more branch-sensitive and can separate distinct dynamical regimes, e.g., one-beat from two-beat responses. Finally, we find that overlapping mean- and std-conditioned manifolds collapse to compact local neighborhoods around held-out original parameters on the inhibition plane and generate temporally similar trajectories within each branch (Fig. 5 C). Consistent with this view, these neighborhoods are approximately ellipsoidal in projection, closer to Gaussian-like clusters than to long compensation strips. Thus, low-order moments do not merely tighten a point estimate; taken together, they localize branch-specific viable parameter sets while revealing the nearby regime structure that perturbs an otherwise smooth manifold geometry.
